draft.title: Specificity and reversibility
card: Training should match the demands of the activity. This includes the energy system used, the muscles used and the type of movement.
Fitness gains are lost if training is reduced or stops. The body adapts to the load it now faces, so gains fade when the load drops.
A long-distance runner gains most from long, steady runs. A sprinter gains most from short, fast efforts, because each sport asks for a different energy system.
An injured athlete who rests for weeks will usually lose some fitness. Light training that suits the sport, where it is safe, can slow this loss.
draft.remember: Train for what the sport demands, and keep training to keep the gains.

a.q: Which training plan best applies specificity for a 100 m sprinter?
opts: Repeated short, fast sprints with full rest between
Steady 10 km runs at a comfortable pace
Long swims at a low, even intensity
Gentle walks on most days of the week
a.why: A 100 m sprint is a short, fast effort, so training should copy that demand. Steady 10 km runs use running, but they do not match the speed and short duration of the event.
a.clue: Match the training to the length and speed of the race.

b.q: Priya is a netball player. She stops training for six weeks after a holiday and finds her fitness has dropped. Which principle explains this?
opts: Reversibility, as gains fade when training stops
Specificity, as her training no longer matched netball
Progressive overload, as she raised her load too fast
Variety, as her sessions had become repetitive
b.why: Fitness gains are lost when training is reduced or stops, which is reversibility. Specificity is tempting, but it is about matching the sport, and Priya's problem was that she did no training at all.
b.clue: Ask what changed: the type of training or the amount of it.

a.best: Repeated short, fast sprints with full rest between

b.best: Reversibility, as gains fade when training stops
